📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A buck is not the only creature in the woods who gets into a “rut” during hunting season. Many hunters adopt a particular method of hunting and never consider changing it, even though the weather and, therefore, the hunting conditions change. For instance, many hunters automatically take to their tree stand and wait. To them, there is simply no other way to hunt. However, on very windy, cold days preceding and during the passage of a cold front, you can sit in a tree stand until you wear the brads off your britches and never see a deer. On the other hand, there are also hunters who would never climb a tree and who insist on still hunting. But on those days when the woods are extremely dry, you can walk to the next county without spotting anything.

According to recent reports, the point is, if you wish to improve your hunting success, you must be adaptable and let prevailing conditions, rather than past practices, determine your hunting methods. While there is much to be said for hunting hard and putting in a good effort, flexibility, rather than fortitude, is the key to good hunting on bad days.

Before devising hunting strategies based upon the weather, it will prove helpful to examine the effects of weather on deer behavior.

As a rule, deer follow their normal routine of bedding, feeding, and moving throughout a wide range of climatic conditions. It is not unusual to see them feeding normally during rain or moving on breezy days. In general, scientists and observers agree about how deer act in relation to weather.

According to Al Berner, a biologist with the Minnesota Department of Natural Resources, “Under typical rainy conditions, there is minimal effect on deer — they will continue to move about normally — but during a freezing rain, they will seek shelter.”.

He also reported that deer continue their normal movements during windy days, but are careful to move into the wind in order to more easily detect danger.

Dean Murphy, chief of the wildlife division of the Missouri Department of Conservation, remarked deer increase their activity somewhat during normal rainy days. This is largely because light is reduced to a level nearer the diurnal range. The amount of daylight on overcast days closely resembles light in the early morning or late afternoon, which is when deer normally move.

It has been revealed that A study recently completed by Scott Hygnstrom, a graduate student at the University of Wisconsin at Stevens Point, revealed some interesting data on buck movements in relation to the wind. The study was conducted with the assistance of members of the Stump Sitters, an organization that studies deer behavior. The results of the study showed that, under perfectly calm wind conditions, there were fewer sightings of bucks than expected. However, under light wind conditions, there were more buck sightings than expected. As wind increased in velocity, buck sightings decreased proportionately.

Recent findings suggest that upon reflection, it seems reasonable that bucks would be more active in a light wind. The wind would make it possible for them to detect danger more easily by catching the scent. At the same time, their ability to hear would not be as diminished as it would be in a strong wind.

It has been revealed that francis X. Leuth, formerly a biologist with the Alabama Department of Conservation and Natural Resources, discovered that the same holds true for whitetails in the Southern United States. Deer continue normal movements in rain and wind unless it becomes very strong or very cold. During such times, deer will hold in cover — sometimes for as long as several days.

All researchers agreed that deer tend to hold up during very heavy weather, whether it be cold rain, wind, sleet, or snow. Most of them also reported increased movement 12 to 36 hours before an advancing front and immediately after its passage.

These authorities also agreed on another point: If hunters continued to hunt during bad weather instead of looking for a warm dry place to wait it out, they would be much more successful.

Before examining various weather conditions and the hunting methods best suited to coping with them, it is important to define the three types of hunting that will be recommended.

Recent findings suggest that the first of these, stand hunting, involves taking a position — either up in a tree or in ground cover — and watching one area for the duration of the hunt. While stand hunting has many advantages, its primary disadvantage is that you are limited in the territory that you can cover. If deer are not moving in the area that you are watching, the hunt is over!

Sources indicate that walk-and-stand hunting means finding concealment on the ground and watching an area for a period of time, then moving on to a newly introduced area. The idea is to watch different kinds of areas to determine where the deer are located. It is somewhat like a bass fisherman trying to establish a pattern by fishing in different kinds of structure, depths, and locations.

Recent findings suggest that stillhunting involves intermittently moving and stopping in a slow, deliberate pattern as you move through the woods. It offers you the opportunity to cover more territory, but it also provides deer with an opportunity to spot you.

In a recent development, some of the conditions that indicate a need to change hunting routines are sudden changes in the weather, days of heavy rain, windy days, and extremely dry conditions. Let’s look at them in detail and see which hunting method best fits each one.

A sudden change in the weather is usually associated with an approaching low-pressure system. For some reason that is not fully understood, all wildlife seem to be more active under these conditions. It is not known for certain whether they know that bad weather is coming and are moving to areas that offer better protection, or if they are eating an extra portion to hold them over for a while. For these reasons, or for some other unexplained reason, their movements increase during these few short hours.

Regardless of the reasons, this type of behavior carries certain implications for hunting techniques. During an approaching front, the walk-and-stand hunter may have a slight advantage. The stand hunter usually places his stand along known trails leading to and from feeding and bedding areas. He also tends to hunt in the morning and the afternoon in order to take advantage of the early/late movement pattern. Because of frequent variations in their movement patterns during an approaching front, deer may not follow their established routines, thus lessening the chance that one will pass by when the stand hunter expects.

Industry observers note that the stillhunter is also at a disadvantage because, although the deer are more active, they are also more alert. Because they are more exposed to danger, they exercise greater caution.

Walk-and-stand hunting offers the best combination of stand and stalk hunting, especially if you stay in the woods all day. The best pattern is to pick a location that offers an open area — not necessarily an open field — and to watch for movement near the edges of cover. For instance, if you can find an open hardwood hollow bordered by pine thickets or honeysuckle, you may find some crossing action or movement along the borders of the thick cover.

Industry observers note that after watching an area for an hour or so, move to another location and repeat the pattern. This allows you to cover a lot of territory during a day, and you are likely to find an area in which the deer are moving.

Recent findings suggest that the most uncomfortable condition to hunt under is rain. If you are going to hunt in the rain, stillhunting offers some advantages. First, you can move very quietly when the ground is wet. Secondly, you can cover more territory. This is often required during rain because you have to go to the deer if they are not moving.

During periods of light rain, the deer’s behavior is hardly affected at all and there would be little need to change a preferred method of hunting under these conditions. However, if you are not skilled at still hunting and wish to learn more about it, this would be an ideal time to give it a try.

Recent findings suggest that if you are not an experienced stillhunter, it is a very awkward and difficult method to develop confidence in. You feel exposed and think that everything in the woods is hiding and watching you. In turn, the temptation is to try to hide behind trees, rocks, and bushes. The problem is that you always see a better place in front of you and you keep moving from one hiding place to another. Soon, you have gone through the area that you were supposed to be hunting and have come out convinced either that nothing was there or that stillhunting is a waste of time. The problem is, you were concentrating on hiding instead of on hunting.

Related: Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Deer Hunting When the Weather Finally Turns Cold.

A few points may prove helpful in learning this highly productive method of hunting. First, move as slowly as possible. Deer see movement more easily than they recognize objects. Second, when you stop, kneel down to blend into the ground cover or lean against a tree so that you are not silhouetted. And third, move less and look more. Study every area of cover and use binoculars! Look for parts of a deer such as an ear, a leg, and especially for the horizontal lines of a back or a belly among the vertical lines of trees or bushes. Many hunters think that binoculars are used primarily to see great distances, but their best use is to find small pieces of a deer in thick cover.

Recent findings suggest that probably the only thing worse than hunting in the rain is hunting when the woods are bone dry. It is more comfortable to the hunter, but it means more difficult hunting. Every movement and crunch of leaves is a signal to the deer to clear out.

Stillhunting and walk-and-stand hunting are difficult, if not impossible, during dry weather, leaving stand hunting as the most logical choice. You may want to choose a ground blind for convenience’s sake but, where it is legal, hunting from a stand in a tree enlarges the area that you can hunt effectively.

Even with the advantage of being able to see better from a tree stand, remember that you cannot see everything at all times. You can only see about one-third of the area at any time and many opportunities for a shot can be missed if you are not alert.

If you want to prove this to yourself, think about how many times you have suddenly noticed a deer standing in the open, 15 or 20 yards from the nearest cover. It did not simply appear on that spot. The deer walked there while you were looking somewhere else. It hurts to think how many go by unnoticed.

The principal way in which dry weather helps the stand hunter is that it cuts down on the area that you have to watch. You patrol the area with both your eyes and your ears. A deer can move more quietly than you can but, when it is dry, even deer will give away their position. On windy days or when the woods are wet, however, deer can slip by without a sound.

One effective technique is to locate your stand on the edge of a field or an open woodland area. You can then hunt the open area with your eyes and the thick woods with your ears, thus covering your hunting area more thoroughly.

Sources indicate that if it is not too wet or too dry, it can always be too windy. Wind has probably saved hunters more ammunition than any other weather condition. I’m not referring to those days when there is a steady breeze blowing — this can be beneficial to the hunter — but rather to those days when it is bitter cold and the wind seems to come from all directions at the same time. On these days, deer will either hold in thick cover and not expose themselves or they will pick up your scent and slip away without your ever knowing that they were there.

Sources indicate that using a buddy system to move deer into the open offers an opportunity to get a shot at a good buck on such days, but the blueprint must be carefully thought out in advance. Pre-planning not only places hunters in the most opportune positions to get the best shot, but also provides a safety measure in that they know where not to shoot.

According to recent reports, for the purpose of illustration, consider a hunting situation in an agricultural area with woods dispersed between fields. The driver should start on the downwind side of the thickest cover in the hope of moving the deer down the hollow into more open areas or across the field into the adjoining woods. If there are fingers of the land protruding out into the fields, they provide natural escape routes. Bucks in particular will cross an open area at its narrowest point.

Hunters should position themselves to cover these routes, but it is better if they take a stand across the field in the adjacent woods, rather than in the same area of woods.

Contrary to appearances, deer do not leave the state when disturbed. They leave the area of disturbance quickly, but soon resume their normal activity at a much slower pace.

According to recent reports, when a deer is jumped and makes its escape across an open area, it will likely slow down once it is out of the immediate area of danger. Often, if you take a stand along an escape route away from the jump area, this will mean a standing or walking shot rather than a quick glimpse of a white flag. Contrary to appearances, deer do not leave the state when disturbed. They leave the area of disturbance rapidly, but soon resume their normal activity at a much slower pace. Hunters should be stationed at other escape points and farther down the hollow in case a jumped deer chooses to move on down the wood line rather than cross the open field.

When attempting to move deer out of cover, it is better to stop occasionally than to walk continuously. Often, a deer will watch from cover and let a hunter walk on by. If you have ever observed deer while driving, you may have seen a similar reaction. If you keep moving, they stand and watch but, if you stop, they move out. The same thing is often true of a continuously moving versus a moving-and-stopping technique of hunting.

A buddy system of moving deer can be devised for any type of terrain you hunt. The key points to remember are to use the system in an area that everyone is familiar with, to identify the stand placements carefully and, for safety’s sake, to coordinate the time and the direction of movements of each person.

Sources indicate that occasionally, even for those of us who are willing to modify our hunting techniques and to learn new ways to hunt on bad days, there are those times when it is neither too wet, too dry, nor too windy. And on those days, even if you don’t see a deer, you can always think, “What a great day to be hunting!”.

This story, “Good Deer Hunting On Bad Days,” appeared in the April 1985 problem of Outdoor Life.

Tech Report: Why You Should Never Underestimate Mule Deer

If you head north and east out of Salt Lake City toward the Wyoming state line you end up in some of the most stunning country in the United States. At first glance, it looks like a semi-arid range of mountains with the exposed shelves of red rock, patches of sage, and grassy benches typical of the Intermountain West at this latitude.

In a recent development, but once you get past the view from the winding highways that snake through this land and gain some elevation on the dirt roads that take you back to more remote areas, you’ll notice something else. These mountains give birth to a surprising number of springs, providing water that ends up supporting a vast amount of life.

The wet country reveals itself in the stands of aspen that grow thick in places you wouldn’t expect, with waist-high grass that contrasts with the blanket of drought-resistant scrub oak that covers much of the terrain.

This almost contradictory mix of moisture, cover, food, and remoteness provides a recipe for great elk and mule deer, and is the reason I’ll return to this country whenever I can, as happened a few weeks ago this fall. I was there on an invitation from Winchester Ammunition to try its newest offering, Supreme Long Range, on my favorite North American game.

There are many reasons mule deer have such a strong claim on my psyche. I love the wild places they call home. The hours spent glassing them is about the most rewarding way to pass time. And I find it infinitely fascinating to watch and study their behavior.

You see, mule deer are a study in contradiction, too. Are their numbers in decline? In many places, without a doubt. They’ve certainly struggled to maintain their hold in much of their traditional range. Housing and energy development disrupt their winter grounds and migration routes. Diseases like CWD have taken their toll, especially with older bucks. We know that blossoming herds of elk and whitetails can outcompete mulies for food and water, putting more pressure on their numbers.

According to recent reports, but they are also resilient and, in some areas, thrive. Good numbers of mule deer live in suburban areas throughout the mountain west. And you can find them in some of the most inhospitable desert regions of North America, and tucked away in other unlikely places.

Though they can seem more docile than their high-strung white-tailed cousins, I have witnessed mule deer put on incredible displays of strength, aggression, and John-Wick-caliber willpower — another contradiction.

Years ago in Colorado, I watched a hunter fail to follow up his shot on a mule deer. The high-shoulder shot dropped the buck where it stood, knocking it senseless. The hunter started celebrating, thinking he had killed it, and when the deer regained its feet the hunter wasn’t ready — and the buck disappeared into the alders. I helped track the deer for several hours through the snow, following a substantial blood trail. We kept going as long as we could after dark but eventually had to call it quits.

The hunter left for the airport and I kept looking for the deer with my good friend Cody while trying to fill my own tag. Two days later, Cody and I spotted the buck tending his does, despite the grievous wound in his upper chest and one ruined leg. He was 500 yards away, skylined on the ridge, and I couldn’t get a shot off before he fled over the mountain.

Recent findings suggest that there was no doubt in my mind the buck was going to die from that injury, but procreation was his sole preoccupation. Despite the obvious pain, and the imminent certainty of death, he would not be deterred.

According to recent reports, that buck spurned death, but I’ve also seen mule deer inflict it. I was hunting in southeast Montana a few years back in mid-November when the rut was in full swing. Bucks were bird-dogging does, scent-checking the ladies, cruising in search of mates, and squaring up against potential rivals.

Usually when two bucks face off they will posture a bit and, after sizing each other up, one will back off before things get too heated. Sometimes they will fight — those antlers aren’t just for decoration — and the vanquished male will make his excuses to be elsewhere.

In this case, the smaller of the deer lost his footing during the scuffle and fell back, rolling on his side. The larger buck lowered his head and drove his antlers into the other’s exposed belly.

The deer on his side flailed his legs in a desperate attempt to get up and escape, but through my binocular I could see the spreading circle of red in the snow as the dominant buck continued the savage attack, never letting up.

After several minutes — it felt like an eternity from my vantage — the buck’s fury was spent and he lifted his head and walked off as the other deer lay still, surrounded by his own gore.

I relate this because it is one thing to enjoy hunting, which I do, but it is another to, on occasion, experience the wild at its most raw and profound.

So, when I got this latest opportunity to test my legs and lungs in the high-country in Utah, I had hopes of encountering a mature buck, and perhaps more.

I was joined on the trip by Kyle Masinelli, the vice president of manufacturing operations at Winchester Ammunition, and a friend and work colleague of mine, Ed Friedman, the editor-in-chief of American Rifleman. Kyle was one of the architects of Winchester Supreme Long Range and a great source of information about it.

As the name implies, Supreme Long Range (SLR for short) is geared toward substantial-game hunting where longer shots might be in the offing, which is often the case when mule deer hunting. This newly introduced ammo uses what Winchester calls their “BC Max” bullet, which is a heavy-for-caliber cup-and-core design with an oversized polymer tip to initiate rapid expansion.

Over the summer, I shot several boxes of this fresh ammunition, chambered in 6.5 Creedmoor, with excellent results in terms of its precision and consistency.

Sources indicate that I gathered 20 shots of data with three different rifles, shooting four 5-shot groups with each. Those twelve 5-shot groups ranged in size from .53 inches to 1.10 inches. The overall average group size was .818 inches.

In a curious coincidence, the mean radius value for each of the three rifles was .32 inches, which is very good for hunting ammunition.

The three rifles I used to gather the data were Proof’s MTR Elevation FDX, which won an Editor’s Choice for best hunting rifle of the year; Seekins Precision’s latest PH3 NRL Hunter, which won an Editor’s Choice for best crossover rifle; and a Seekins Precision SIC Short Action, which won’t be officially launched until early 2027.

For the hunt itself, I went a different route, taking a Winchester XPR chambered in 6.8 Western. The XPR has been a perennial choice of ours for an entry-level hunting rifle. It is a no-frills bolt-action that delivers good performance. In its most basic black synthetic stock trim it can be had for less than $600 fresh.

It has been revealed that while I’ve shot plenty of XPRs over the years, I hadn’t had as much time with the 6.8 Western. I shot this souped-up .270 Winchester a bit when it was first rolled out in 2021, but had never done a deep dive on the cartridge or taken it hunting.

I didn’t have as much trigger time with the XPR and the ammunition as I would have liked before rolling into camp, but I did establish a solid zero prior to making the drive from Montana to Utah and knew that the 175-grain 6.8mm SLR bullets were exiting my 22-inch barrel right at 2,700 fps.

Industry observers note that we were hunting with the R&K Hunting Firm, which has a base camp in Coalville, Utah, and I confirmed my dope on targets they had there. With three shots, I checked my point of impact at 200, 500, and 700 yards, the bullets ringing the center of the steel each time.

Our hunting camp was another hour’s drive into the mountains, most of it off-road, and much of it pitted with craters like small bomb impacts.

But the camp itself was an alpine Shangri-La. The main lodge was a cozy wood structure where the hunters stayed, with a series of small cabins for the guides, and other out buildings, all overlooking a post-card scene of a small lake surrounded by golden-leafed quakies and distant mountains.

Those mountains were where we hunted.

Sources indicate that kyle and I spent the first day with our guides, two young brothers named Keston and Kandon Mosher, glassing the heights. In the afternoon, we spotted two excellent bucks engaged in pre-rut posturing.

According to recent reports, from nearly a mile away we watched the bucks through our optics. One of the bucks appeared to have a larger, darker body and a heavier rack. The other buck was mature as well, seemingly younger, but with larger antlers. Both were stunning.

In a recent development, we watched them circle each other a bit in a small clearing between stands of alders. We needed to move quickly, because the cover around them was thick, it was getting late, and we were losing light.

Sources indicate that we grabbed our packs and guns and hoofed up the mountain as fast as we could. It took about half an hour of hard climbing to get to the knob we wanted to set up on. That put us within 800 yards of where we’d last seen the deer.

Sources indicate that assuming we spotted them again, we’d make a final strategy. But that didn’t happen. We glassed the ridge until dark. We could see many of the other deer we’d been watching, but the bucks had vanished. As has happened to me so many times while going after major mule deer, they’d given us the slip.

We returned to the base of that mountain ahead of sunrise, peering into the cover as the light came up. With each passing minute, we took in more ground.

The mountain was actually a long, fairly flat ridge running north to south that topped out at 9,200 feet, and encompassed five separate large drainages. From end-to-end it spanned over three miles. The middle section seemed to hold the most animals, but we frequently spotted elk and deer at the northern and southern edges too.

Sources indicate that early on, Keston caught a flash of antler in an alder thicket not far from the top of the ridge. We all trained our optics on the spot and after a bit the lighter-colored buck stepped into the open. We easily identified him based on his coloration and the picture-perfect four-point frame he carried above his head.

According to recent reports, he was feeding on his own about 350 yards from where we’d seen him the previous afternoon. About 30 yards below him was a doe and two fawns, also munching on grass. The other big buck was nowhere to be seen.

In a recent development, there was no way to get to him from below. Even if we could approach from that direction without busting him he’d be out of sight until we stepped into the same clearing. That clearly wouldn’t work. Plus it would take well over an hour and a half to hike up there at which point he’d certainly be gone even if we were as stealthy as ninjas.

Industry observers note that instead, we hiked back down to our side-by-side and took a long looping route to the top of the ridge. From this latest vantage, the terrain presented more of a challenge than I would have guessed. Looking down, I could see benches and pockets of cover that were invisible from lower down. This included small natural ponds and abundant feed. An animal could move through that all day and never reveal itself to a hunter glassing from below.

We parked well away from where we saw the buck last and snuck along the spine until we were above his feeding spot. We crept toward the edge and peered down the slope.

Recent findings suggest that at this point the wind shifted so it was coming from directly behind us. We saw the doe and her fawns scoot out of the pocket, having clearly caught our scent.

In a recent development, but the buck should have been between us and them, and if he followed a similar escape route, I would get a shot. We held tight for a quarter hour but saw no sign of him. He’d obviously slipped away in a safer, more hidden direction.

In a recent development, I wasn’t surprised. Mule deer get a bad rap for acting dumb during the rut. And it’s true that some bucks seem to throw caution to the wind when love is in the air. But in my experience I’ve seen more evidence of their clever and well-honed survival instincts preserving them from eager hunters, especially when it comes to truly mature bucks.

That afternoon we returned to the base of the ridge. We set up beneath the knob from the previous night because we didn’t want to overcommit and potentially bust the bucks in case they had moved lower down the mountain.

It wasn’t long before we spotted a new buck working its way down a drainage to our right. He was a handsome 4×4 with eyeguards, and Kyle wanted to take him.

He set his .300 Win. Mag. in a tripod and shot the buck at 350 yards from a kneeling position. The bullet was perfectly placed and the buck ran a few steps and tumbled over. Kyle, Keston, and Kandon (which sounds not unlike a law firm) took off to recover the buck while I stayed behind to keep glassing.

By the time Keston returned we had about an hour left of shooting light. As luck would have it, we caught sight of the light-colored deer trying to sneak off to the south.

With the pressure we’d applied to the north half of the ridge that morning and afternoon (Kyle’s deer was in the same drainage as the bench where we spotted the buck after first light) I wasn’t surprised to see the older deer trying to put some distance between us and him.

According to recent reports, once again it was a race against the falling light. Keston and I took off up the mountain to get within range before dark.

In a recent development, we hiked for 20 minutes to an exposed point that gave us a good view. Keston found the deer again, walking to our left and down toward a thick stand of aspen in a steep draw, where he was about to disappear.

Industry observers note that I ranged the deer at 616 yards and got prone, deploying my bipod and setting the butt of the XPR on my shooting bag. The wind, which had been howling earlier in the day, was calming down, but still needed to be accounted for.

In a recent development, I dialed elevation into my scope, held left .4 mil for the wind, and broke the shot. The deer dropped as if poleaxed, kicked a bit, and then lay still. I watched him through my scope with a fresh round chambered until I was sure he was dead.

By the time we got to the vicinity of the deer it was pitch black. Finding an animal under these conditions can be difficult. And while technology is often a two-edged affairm in this case it was a godsend.

For the last year, I’ve been using Leupold’s BX-6 rangefinding binocular in shooting competitions and while hunting. I won’t go into all its virtues here, but one feature that’s a game changer is its ability to range a spot and have it drop a pin into a map, like onX Hunt.

That pin led us right to the buck, saving us who knows how much time stumbling around the dark.

Every hunting bullet has the same end goal, which is to inflict massive tissue damage so that the animal quickly bleeds out, shutting the central nervous system down. (Alternatively, a bullet can strike the CNS directly, with a brain or spinal shot, killing the animal that way.).

Industry observers note that how a bullet accomplishes this depends heavily on its construction. Bonded bullets, for instance, are meant to mushroom to a degree, while retaining weight and penetrating deeply.

The BC Max bullet takes a different approach. The large polymer tip on the projectile initiated quick and violent bullet upset. The entrance hole, in the upper portion of the chest, was about two inches across and busted two ribs on the way in.

I could tell the bullet fragmented significantly based on three things: that large entrance wound, the massive tissue damage observed on the deer’s lungs, and the fact that the bullet didn’t penetrate the off side of the ribcage.

We quartered the deer and took backstraps, loins, and neck meat without gutting it, so I didn’t try to recover what was left of the bullet, though I doubt it would have been much.

Of all the substantial mule deer I’ve shot over my career, this one comes closest to the Platonic ideal. He’s a large, clean four-point, with deep, nearly identical, forks front and back, has a tall boxy frame, carries good mass throughout his rack, and has nice eye guards to boot. If one were to draw an idealized symmetrical mule deer, it would look a lot like this one.

Industry observers note that I never take an animal like this for granted. He was a wily deer and had given us the slip a couple times already, and was about to make it a third. And, of course, there was his older cousin, that darker, heavier brute, who only demonstrated himself once.

Industry observers note that we were the last deer hunters on that mountain this season. And my fingers are crossed that the other big buck, and his kin, make it through the winter.

Recent findings suggest that I don’t say that because I expect to hunt that spot again. There’s very little chance that will happen. But I do hope some other hunter, who loves these animals the way I do, at least gets to encounter that buck and possibly take him home.

That’s the shared dream all avid mule deer hunters have, and is what draws us to the mountains each fall in pursuit of America’s most interesting, complicated, and magnificent species of game.

Two Borrowed Shotguns, Two Record Bucks, and the Best Opening Morning in Ohio History

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3657 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This story, “The Luck of Irish Ridge,” appeared in the December 1966 issue of Outdoor Life.
  • In a recent development, the 1965 deer season in the hill country of southeastern Ohio was 15 minutes old, but the woods were silent.
  • Recent findings suggest that but I didn’t want to risk moving, now that shooting was legal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This story, “The Luck of Irish Ridge,” appeared in the December 1966 issue of Outdoor Life. While it was an incredible deer, Ohio is an incredible state for big whitetails. Allison’s buck is now ranked 41 among Ohio’s biggest typical bucks.

In a recent development, the 1965 deer season in the hill country of southeastern Ohio was 15 minutes old, but the woods were silent. I was hunkered down with my back against a tree in an open place on the side of a big ridge. The place was too open, but I hadn’t realized that when I sat down there just before the opening hour of 9 o’clock. A deer could see me a mile away, I told myself.

Recent findings suggest that but I didn’t want to risk moving, now that shooting was legal. Anyway, I didn’t know where there was a better stand. So I just sat still, hoping for the best.

It was a clear November morning, frosty but promising to warm up later. Most of the timber on the side of the ridge was oak. That meant acorns, and acorns are likely to mean deer. Maybe I hadn’t picked such a bad spot after all. It was warm and pleasant there in the sun. I’d wait awhile and see what happened.

It has been revealed that suddenly, the stillness was shattered by a shot. A few seconds later another one rapped out. Though I wasn’t sure which direction the shots came from, I decided it was some hunter over the ridge behind me. I didn’t dream what had happened. The woods got quiet again, and then bluejays started to holler on the ridge.

I’d hunted deer only three years before this and was too inexperienced to know what those noisy bluejays meant. I’ll know next time.

The next thing I heard was something moving in the dry oak leaves behind me. It didn’t sound big enough for a deer, but it startled me. I swiveled my head slowly for a look. It seemed to take me an eternity to turn my head and body without making any sudden motions or noise.

Whatever I was hearing kept coming, walking slowly and deliberately. I finally got twisted into position and eased one eye around the trunk of the tree I’d been sitting against.

What I saw then literally took my breath away.

In a recent development, walking slowly down the slope, only 15 or 20 yards away and coming almost straight toward me, was a giant buck with the biggest rack I’d ever seen. The morning sun glinted on his polished, brown tines, and he looked as if he were wearing the bleached roots of an upturned stump on his head. I didn’t know it then, but I was looking at a whitetail deer that was better than any that had ever been killed in Ohio.

He stopped for a second and looked back up the ridge, the direction he’d come from, and I remember thinking that somebody over there must have spooked him. Then he turned my way and came on, walking calmly and unafraid. To this day, I don’t know why I didn’t have the worst case of buck fever a young deer hunter ever had.

Industry observers note that my dad, Don Allison, and I had left home the previous evening and driven to Wellston, where we were to stay for the hunting season with dad’s friend and hunting partner, Jim Arthur. We live near South Solon, in the flat prairie country about 40 miles southwest of Columbus. Dad runs a 232-acre farm on some of the nation’s richest land. He handles a herd of 20 Black Angus cows and their calves and feeds out about 350 hogs a year.

I was 17 years old at the time and a senior at Madison South High School south of London.

I’ve hunted with dad ever since I could carry a gun. We get rabbits, pheasants, and fox squirrels in the farming areas around home, and the last few years we’ve made trips for grouse to the hill country of eastern Ohio. In 1962, dad took me deer hunting for the first time.

The deer season is the only real vacation dad takes. He started hunting deer in 1944, the second year Ohio had an open season, and has missed only one fall since, except for years when the season was closed. But he’s been plagued by hard luck. In almost 20 years of hunting, up to last fall, he’d never killed a deer.

The closest he ever came was getting a shot at a doe, but he confessed that buck fever — if a female deer can give you buck fever — got the best of him that time, and he scored a clean miss. He loves to hunt, though, and has never gotten discouraged.

“I’ll be lucky one of these years,” he always said, not knowing just how lucky.

Recent findings suggest that my record was no better. In three falls of hunting, I hadn’t even seen a deer. But, like dad, I was sure my time would come.

Ohio’s 1965 gun season on deer was a restricted one, varying from region to region according to herd conditions and the management plans of the state game men. In the northwestern counties, level farm country, there was a three-day either-sex season, but hunters had to have in advance a landowner’s written permission to hunt in order to get a deer permit.

In the hill country of southeastern Ohio, where we’ve always hunted, there was a bucks-only season beginning on Monday, November 8, and lasting four days. Hunting hours were from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., and only shotguns loaded with slugs or pumpkin balls were legal, as in the past.

Recent findings suggest that as November drew near, dad and I both developed the usual deer-hunting itch. It’s hard to tell anybody how much our annual whitetail hunt means to us. But for a time, it didn’t look as if either of us could make it. Dad had almost 100 acres of corn to pick. Deer season was about a month earlier than usual, and the picking job would be no more than well started by November 8. If he took time off to go hunting, wintry weather could set in before he finished the corn picking.

“I’m going,” he finally told us, “even if I have to pick corn when the snow’s blowing.”.

My problem was basketball — I had a good chance to make the school team. We’d practiced about a week when deer season rolled around, and the rule was that anybody who missed practice unexcused would be dropped from the squad.

It was a fair rule, and I knew going deer hunting wasn’t a valid excuse. If I went, my basketball career would end before it started. But the hunt was too much to pass up.

“If you’re going,” I told dad, “so am I.”.

There was one other problem. We both had gun trouble. Dad usually shoots a Model 12 Winchester 12 gauge that he’s had for years. But it was out of order, so he borrowed a 12 gauge Remington autoloader. I was getting ready to buy a fresh shotgun, so I borrowed a Browning 16 gauge automatic on trial. We’d both be using guns we’d had little chance to get familiar with.

“Well, if we see deer and miss,” dad noted with a grin, “at least we’ve got a good alibi.”.

Dad hunted for many years in the Shawnee State Forest, along the Ohio River west of Portsmouth. It’s a 60,000-acre tract, rugged and steep, with oak-covered ridges and few roads. It’s easy to get lost there unless you’re familiar with the hills. Other parts of Ohio may have more deer, but many hunters prefer this wild country.

It has been revealed that dad had another reason for hunting there. It was the favorite spot of a good friend of his, Belvin Adams. Adams lived in Wheelersburg, only a short distance away, and he and a party of his friends had hunted the Shawnee for years.

Industry observers note that but three years ago, the rubber organization Adams works for moved him to Indonesia. Since then, Jim Arthur, who lives in Wellston and had worked with Adams, has invited dad and me to stay at his home and hunt with his party in the Raccoon and Zaleski state forests, in Vinton County. These forests have a combined area of about 30,000 acres, and the timberlands are mixed with some farming acreage, making good deer range. That was where dad and I would go for the 1965 season.

According to recent reports, jim Arthur has a son, Steve, who’s my age and, like me, was a senior in high school then. We have a lot in common, especially our enthusiasm for deer hunting.

In a recent development, we got to Wellston Sunday evening, too late to scout the area we intended to hunt. And Jim Arthur told us that he’d been too busy to do any looking in recent weeks. That meant we’d start cold on opening day, not knowing where deer were hanging out or where their feeding grounds and travel routes were. But at least we’d hunted the general area for three years and knew the lay of the land.

Industry observers note that we sat up late that night, as we usually do the night before the season opens, recalling other hunts, laying looks, guessing what kind of luck we’d have. And the longer we talked, the higher our hunting fever mounted.

Sources indicate that we turned in finally, got a few hours of sleep, and were up early, checking our equipment and taking care of last-minute details. About 8 o’clock, though we couldn’t start hunting for another hour, we drove out to a long hogback called Irish Ridge, between the Raccoon and Little Raccoon creeks, a few miles southeast of Wellston. We didn’t want another party to beat us to our stands, and we wanted to be set at 9 o’clock in case hunters around us began moving deer.

I followed an abandoned township road that wound along the side of the ridge. Steve was quite a way below me on the slope, his dad was walking the crest of the ridge, and my dad was about halfway down on the other side. A few minutes before 9, I picked the oak-tree stand I described in the beginning and settled down.

I heard the two shots and heard the bluejays yell. Then that huge buck came walking slowly down the ridge.

According to recent reports, I eased into shooting position slowly and carefully, and I raised the Browning just as cautiously. The buck took a few more steps, reached the old, leaf-strewn road, and stopped to look around. He was only 30 feet away. I had time to remind myself that I was using an unfamiliar gun and to remember how it worked. I pushed the safety off and leveled on him.

Recent findings suggest that dad had told me many times to shoot for the spine when my chance came. I remembered that advice now and followed it. My 16 gauge rifled slug smashed through the deer’s backbone just behind the shoulders, and he fell like a ton of bricks. But he pulled himself half up on his forelegs, so I did the second thing dad had always instructed me to do.

“Once you get a deer down,” he’d said, “shoot for the heart and finish him in a hurry.”.

Dad had read a lot about deer hunting and talked with many hunters, and it never occurred to me that there was anything strange about his having such firm opinions, even though he’d never killed a deer. His advice proved itself again now. I put in a heart shot, and this time the buck didn’t get up.

It has been revealed that he was still thrashing around, though, working himself downhill. And suddenly I saw that he was going to fall over a low cliff. I watched, and my heart sank as he rolled over the edge and disappeared. The cliff muffled his fall, and I ran to the edge, almost afraid to look. If part of that magnificent rack had broken, I’d be sick.

He lay dead at the foot of the cliff, 20 or 30 feet below. One front leg, broken in the fall, stuck out at an angle. I couldn’t see enough of his horns to tell about them.

In a recent development, I waited long enough to be sure he was dead and then found a place where I could climb down. I took a good look at his head and breathed a gusty sigh of relief. Not a single point was damaged. Was I thankful!

After my heart stopped thumping, I started wondering how we’d ever get him up to the old road. We couldn’t take him up the cliff, and there was a very steep grade wherever I looked. But before I had time to think much, I heard Steve call. I yelled back, and in a few minutes he joined me. When he saw what I’d shot, he was about as excited as I was, and I guess I was as proud as anybody in Ohio right then.

It has been revealed that I had never dressed a deer, so I asked Steve to stay with the buck while I went to find dad. I climbed to the top of the ridge and, before going much farther, heard voices down in a brushy gully. I shouted.

“Come on down,” dad said. When I got there, he and Jim were standing over a mighty big buck, and dad had the happiest look on his face that I’d ever seen.

He had killed his deer almost exactly as I’d taken mine and not more than five minutes earlier. The two shots I’d heard were his.

He’d walked in along the side of the ridge and found the kind of stand he was looking for. He was about to sit when he heard something rustling the dry leaves behind him. When he turned around, there came a big buck, walking downhill toward him.

The deer didn’t see him, and dad waited until it was abreast of him and only 40 feet away. Then he floored it with a spine shot. After falling, it slid down into a gully and out of sight. Dad ran up to the edge and saw that the deer was still kicking, so he finished it off with a slug through the heart.

“I got one the same way over on the other side of the ridge,” I blurted out. Then I took another look at dad’s buck and added, “Only mine’s bigger.”.

We shook hands and thumped each other on the back, and I don’t believe there were ever two happier hunters in the deer woods. After 20 years of waiting and trying for dad, and four for me, it was hard to believe that we’d killed two bucks, both big busters, in the first half hour of the season, within a few hundred yards of each other, and with borrowed guns. What luck!

As far as we’ve been able to find out, we were the first father-and-son team ever to take two record-book trophies — both of our bucks turned out to be that — in a single season anywhere in the country, to say nothing of getting them in such a hurry. Those certainly were 20 magic minutes.

Jim and dad had been trying to figure out a way to hang dad’s buck. With three pairs of hands to hoist and heave, it wasn’t too hard. As soon as it was done, Jim started back with me to dress my deer while dad went to work on his.

We found we couldn’t hang my buck. The slope was too steep, and there were no suitable trees. But Jim, Steve, and I pulled and skidded it around so that the head was uphill. Then Jim showed me how to field-dress a deer where it lay.

Sources indicate that four other men, friends of Jim’s and dad’s, had started out to hunt with us that morning. Three of them were nearby, heard us yelling, and came to help. We needed them. Even with part of the crew pulling on ropes and the rest lifting and pushing, it was all the seven of us could do to get my buck up the slope to the old road.

We left him there, went after dad’s, and skidded it to the ridge top. Then we dragged the two bucks out to the cars. It was past noon when we finished and headed to town for lunch.

We hung our two deer side by side in Jim Arthur’s yard. Cars drove by in a steady stream the rest of the day as word of our trophies got around Wellston. Dad phoned home, and mother and Joan Mace, wife of a neighboring farmer, agreed to drive down in the Mace pickup and take the deer home.

By the time they got to the Arthur home, there was so much traffic around it that they had to park two blocks away. We cleared a path through the traffic, loaded the deer, and drove back to the state checking station for the required check.

Industry observers note that the bucks were weighed the next morning. Field-dressed, with heart and lungs out, mine tallied 253 pounds, dad’s 240. According to the conversion table we used to estimate their live weight, mine would have gone just over 300 when I shot it, dad’s almost 290.

It has been revealed that we took the heads to Max Shipley, a Columbus taxidermist. The minute he saw them, he phoned Merrill Gilfillan of the Ohio Division of Wildlife, to whom I have related this story. Merrill is an official scorer for both the Buckeye Massive Bucks Club and the Boone and Crockett Club.

Recent findings suggest that both were typical-whitetail racks, and to our delight both made the record lists of both clubs. After the required 60-day shrinkage period, mine scored a whopping 187 6/8, dad’s 160 2/8. Up until this point, we hadn’t realized how big our bucks really were.

Recent findings suggest that according to the 1964 edition of the Boone and Crockett Club’s Records of North American Big Game, mine is the biggest typical whitetail ever killed in Ohio and rates a place among the first 10 on the list. I have entered it in the 1966-67 Boone and Crockett competition. Officials tell me that any deer scoring that high has a very good chance of winning first place among typical whitetails in that competition.

For some reason, Ohio produces far more than its fair share of big whitetail heads. It’s by no means one of the big deer-kill states. The herd numbers only an estimated 20,000 to 30,000, and in recent years hunters have killed fewer than 1,000 annually, as compared with kills of 100,000 and more in such leading whitetail states as Minnesota, Michigan, and Wisconsin.

Sources indicate that yet there has been no recent season that did not see three to five Ohio bucks make the Boone and Crockett record list in either the typical or nontypical category. In six open seasons between 1956 and 1962 (deer hunting was closed in 1961), 24 Ohio deer qualified for that honor, 13 of them typical racks, 11 nontypical.

We shook hands and thumped each other on the back, and I don’t believe there were ever two happier hunters in the deer woods.

And in the 1958-59 big-game competition sponsored by the Boone and Crockett Club, Ohio whitetails — one with a typical rack and the other nontypical — won first place in both those categories.

In a recent development, the nontypical deer was killed in Ashtabula County in 1957 by James L. Clark of Ashtabula, and the typical buck in Harrison County a year later. Dr. James Rumbaugh and John Ruyan of Westerville shared the honors on that one, both having shot at it. Clark, in collaboration with Merrill Gilfillan, told the story of those two busters in “How I Got No. 1 Deer,” in the November, 1960, problem of Outdoor Life.

In addition, about 180 heads have qualified in the last 10 years for a place on the record list of the Buckeye Major Bucks Club, a state organization sponsored by the Division of Wildlife. Minimum score requirement for this club is 140, just 20 points below that of the Boone and Crockett Club.

Game men believe that Ohio’s phenomenal showing is due to a favorable combination of cropland and woodland — providing an abundance of top-quality deer food — plus certain trace minerals in the soil and hunting rules that have prevented both overhunting and overcrowding of the range. Vinton County, for example, where we hunted, is more than two thirds woods and brush but does have some farmland, including cornfields, in the valleys. That’s likely to mean substantial, healthy deer.

According to recent reports, read Next: The Incredible Hunt for the C.W. Shelton Buck, One of the Widest Bucks in the World.

Recent findings suggest that as for the consequences of our hunt, dad fared better than I did. He finished his corn picking in cold weather but without any real problems. But I missed out on something pretty special. Our basketball team turned out to be a championship outfit, winning the Darby Valley League pennant and all but the last game in the district tournament. But I wasn’t on it.

Dad and I were both disappointed about that, but if I were doing it over again, I’d make the same choice. I can’t ever be sorry I went on that deer hunt.

Public-Land Sales, Energy Dominance, and Data Centers: What Interior’s Master Plan Really Means for Outdoorsmen

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Less than two months after a dinner at the White House with leaders of hunting and angling groups in which President Trump and Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum confirmed support for conservation priorities, Burgum has formalized the Trump administration’s intends to shrink the federal estate and to site industrial data centers and energy infrastructure on America’s public lands.
  • Sources indicate that as we reported last week, the intentions are outlined in the Department of the Interior’s five-year strategic blueprint that extends through 2030.
  • The 28-page initiative is short on details but long on statements about the department’s role in domestic energy “dominance,” “unleashing the potential” of America’s public lands, and pursuit of “public-private partnerships.” In addition to his role at the helm of the Department of Interior, Burgum also chairs the White House National Energy Dominance Council.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Less than two months after a dinner at the White House with leaders of hunting and angling groups in which President Trump and Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum confirmed support for conservation priorities, Burgum has formalized the Trump administration’s intends to shrink the federal estate and to site industrial data centers and energy infrastructure on America’s public lands.

Sources indicate that as we reported last week, the intentions are outlined in the Department of the Interior’s five-year strategic blueprint that extends through 2030. The document serves as a blueprint for implementing the priorities of the Bureau of Land Management, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Bureau of Reclamation, National Park Service, and Bureau of Indian Affairs, among other Interior agencies.

The 28-page initiative is short on details but long on statements about the department’s role in domestic energy “dominance,” “unleashing the potential” of America’s public lands, and pursuit of “public-private partnerships.” In addition to his role at the helm of the Department of Interior, Burgum also chairs the White House National Energy Dominance Council.

The few detailed directives contained in the five-year initiative note Interior’s intention to “decrease the size of the federal estate by offering to states, localities, and Tribes the opportunity to purchase federal lands” in order to better focus the department’s resources on “nationally significant federal lands.” The strategic plan further emphasizes Interior’s pursuit of “strategic rights-of-way agreements, land exchanges, and direct transfer of lands in support of reliable energy production and transport.”.

Recent findings suggest that and the initiative specifically calls for redirecting revenue from the Land and Water Conservation Fund, which is funded by offshore oil and gas leasing revenue, to private-land easements rather than outright purchase of land by the government for recreation and resource purposes. The fund provides about $900 million annually to acquire land, improve existing properties, and invest in communities’ cultural and outdoor recreation assets.

Recent findings suggest that the Department of Interior’s initiative’s mention of possible land sales provoked quick push-back from lawmakers from both parties who recall the tsunami of opposition to inclusion of federal land sales as part of the 2025 Major Beautiful Bill. Language that would have funded tax breaks by selling large parcels of public land was eventually withdrawn from that bill, which was later signed into law by Trump.

Both of Montana’s Republican senators, including retiring Sen. Steve Daines, who sits on the powerful Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, told the news agency Politico that they were not consulted on Interior’s strategic initiative and would oppose the idea of land sales. Yesterday, Burgum, responding to growing criticism of the land-sale language, told Fox News that national parks would not be sold. He called public-land supporters’ reaction to the strategic plan “manufactured hysteria.”.

But the renewed conversation around the topic, along with the initiative’s focus on energy development and investment in “Super Intelligence” infrastructure, raises the question: How seriously should America’s hunters, anglers, and outdoor enthusiasts take Interior’s blueprint, or is the strategic plan simply glossy “shelfware” that will be ignored as a new Congress convenes in January and other priorities shove it to the background?

It has been revealed that “The thing about these aims is that they don’t really hold a lot of authority,” claims a government affairs executive who didn’t have permission to speak on the record. “The agencies have to put them out periodically, but this is not a chapter-and-verse regulatory document or a change in the statute. Instead, you can read it as a sort of statement of purpose.”.

In order to execute sales or transfers of federal land, they note, the Interior would have to undertake a formal land-use planning process with opportunities for public comment. That’s a core provision of the Federal Land Policy and Management Act. But some conservation groups are signaling that a new bill working its way through the lame-duck Congress this week, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act would undermine many of those land-disposal requirements. And the administration’s undercutting of the BLM’s Resource Management Prepares further weakens norms that have kept land transfers a rare exception.

Related: Senate Poised to Vote on Affordability Bill that Hunters, Anglers Worry Is a Trojan Horse for Public-Land Rollbacks.

A more present worry isn’t outright land sales, which are overwhelmingly opposed by America’s hunters and anglers. It’s the long-term lease of federal lands for hyper-scale data centers and energy facilities, notes Randy Newberg, a longtime public-land advocate and podcaster.

“Within this vision proposal is an awful lot of what I’d call greasing the skids for private development of public land, which in all aspects is quasi-ownership of public land,” indicates Newberg. “Given the transactional nature of this administration, I worry about sweetheart deals that help your buddy who is friends with the president or cabinet secretary to develop data centers or oil and gas facilities, you name it.”.

Newberg indicates the outcome is the opposite of conservation.

“Under that vision document, you can just about bet that our public lands will become far more industrialized than any of us probably ever expected.”.

In a recent development, no one should be especially surprised to see land transfer discussed at this vision-document level. After all, it’s a plank in Republican Party platforms in several states, including Montana, where party leaders last summer amended the position confirming their support for public-land transfer but also encouraging public access.

Montana’s GOP ratified the updated platform in June to read “Support transferring federally managed lands to the state with a transition plan and continued public access.” The previous version had simply encouraged transfer of federal lands to the states “in order to secure statehood equality and provide for better management of public lands.”.

According to recent reports, interestingly, even the polarizing Project 2025 document, organized by the Heritage Foundation to prioritize policies of the incoming second Trump administration, doesn’t explicitly advocate transferring federal land. On the other hand, the document’s section outlining Department of the Interior priorities — maximizing energy production on federal lands, rolling back protections for national monuments, and weakening environmental reviews — are all reprised in Burgum’s five-year plan.

One of the few times the current Congress pushed back on administrative priorities in the second Trump term was to remove the land-transfer provisions of the Substantial Beautiful Bill. That opposition was led by Montana Rep. Ryan Zinke (R), the former Secretary of Interior in Trump’s first term, who later founded the Public Lands Caucus in Congress. But the next Congress, with majority Democrats energized by successes in this month’s mid-term election, is likely to demand oversight and review of federal agencies, including Interior.

In a recent development, one of the incoming freshmen, Democrat Sam Forstag, took Zinke’s western Montana seat by about 9 points. It’s the first time in 30 years that Montanans elected a Democrat to represent them in the U.S. House of Representatives. Forstag is a U.S. Forest Service smokejumper and union leader who ran on issues of affordability and against politics that “puts working people last.”.

Speaking from Washington, D.C., yesterday as he rushed between meetings and caucused with fellow freshmen, Forstag says that public-land management has the potential to be a rare bipartisan issue.

“The notion of shrinking the federal estate and selling off our public lands sounds damned concerning to me,” Forstag noted. “I think particularly as we’re seeing a change of leadership in Congress, this is the concern I see as having the most potential for not just bringing the [Democrat] caucus together but building bipartisan support. Republicans who may not have stood up publicly when we needed them the last couple of years are coming around that when it comes to actual people, public lands are not a partisan issue. They’re one of the last places where you don’t have to be rich to get access to it. [Public lands] are a reason Montana is a place worth living while costs skyrocket.”.

Forstag, who hopes to land an assignment on the House Committee on Natural Resources, says he considers talk about selling or leasing federal lands for data centers or energy infrastructure to be a “distraction.”.

Read Next: The Rush to Build Data Centers on Public Lands Is Worse Than You Thought.

“The way you fix affordability isn’t selling off what little bit working people still have,” he states. “The way you fix affordability is not building a data center in the wilderness. It’s getting private equity the hell out of housing, and reinvesting in things like Community Development Block Grants, which have been systematically underfunded for decades while billionaires got tax cuts.”.

According to recent reports, with groceries and gas so pricey, it’s no wonder so many of us are turning to Costco. Everyone knows the warehouse is a deal machine for electronics, home goods, and tires, but this time of year, the aisles are also stocked with a surprising array of ski gear at steep discounts.

Plenty of skiers assume outdoor gear from major-box stores and other non-specialty retailers can’t be trusted. At Costco, that’s not necessarily true. The warehouse pulls in items from brands skiers know, like Smith, Spyder, Dakine, Eddie Bauer, and Head, and its seasoned members know a steal when they see one. A Spyder full-zip sweater jacket for $30 or less? That goes straight in the cart. Buy now, try on at home: Costco’s “satisfaction guaranteed” return policy means you can easily take back whatever doesn’t work out.

In a recent development, the catch: buying ski gear from a warehouse means making compromises. A specialty ski shop has gear with premium features like name-brand insulation and weatherproof materials (and premium prices to match). If you’re outside for hours in gnarly weather, you may need those technical features to stay warm and dry. But casual skiers, beginners, and kids will find plenty of choices at Costco, and experts can find some gems, too. It’s the perfect place for a comfy fleece, a reasonably priced heated vest, a MIPS helmet, affordable gloves and goggles, and après-ski accessories. SKI recommends the following items, but act fast because, like a powder day, the goods won’t last.

Fine print: you’ll need a Costco membership to snag any of these, so factor the annual fee into your budget.

Smith is a specialty-shop staple, so finding the Survey on the Costco website is a legit surprise. This all-mountain lid pairs MIPS with Koroyd zones that keep the weight down. An integrated ChromaPop visor stands in for goggles and works with glasses, and a dial fine-tunes the fit.

Compromise: There really isn’t one. You get a top-shelf helmet at Costco pricing (it retails for around $260 elsewhere). If you weren’t a visor-helmet person before now, maybe you just became one?

This is the budget way to get a MIPS-equipped helmet on your head, and it hits the feature checklist. Three-stage vents let you dump heat on sunny laps, the earpads come out when spring arrives, and a built-in goggle lock keeps most goggles from sliding off the back. An adjustable retention system helps dial in the fit, and it comes in four sizes, small through extra large.

Compromise: You get the safety and venting, but not the luxe features of a premium helmet, like a plush lining or a magnetic chin buckle.

According to recent reports, magnetic lens swap systems are usually a perk of pricier goggles, but Nordik includes one in these affordable goggles. The HOD’s magnetic system lets you pop lenses in and out in seconds, and the box includes a second, low-light lens so you’re covered when the sun disappears. The oversized spherical lens has anti-fog treatment and UV400 protection, and the roomy OTG frame fits over large glasses and runs medium to large. A carrying case is thrown in, too.

Compromise: You’re not getting top-of-the-line lenses with light-adapting tech, so you’ll swap lenses by hand when conditions change.

When it comes to ski mittens, leather is king, and getting a deerskin outer at Costco prices is a serious bargain. Deerskin naturally sheds water and wind and holds up to season after season of abuse, the kind of toughness synthetic shells struggle to match. These pair that shell with 150-gram 3M Thinsulate and a waterproof, breathable insert. The extended gauntlet cuff, with an adjustable strap and cinch cord, seals out powder.

Compromise: You’re not getting a branded waterproof membrane like Gore-Tex, so don’t count on premium storm performance.

According to recent reports, you can outfit the entire family with Head’s ski gloves thanks to a size run ranging from XS to XL. With a combination of lightweight and breathable insulation and a waterproof/windproof insert, the gloves keep hands warm on milder ski days, with an exterior zippered pocket for handwarmers. Touchscreen technology means you can access your smartphone without removing your gloves.

Compromise: If you spend less than $25 on gloves, don’t expect them to hold up to prolonged exposure to super cold temps or wet weather. (You’d have to spend at least $100 more for that.) Durability may be a weakness too, as the soft polyester material on the palm could peel off with use.

According to recent reports, dakine, born in Hawaii in 1979 and now a fixture in ski and snowboard shops, is another name you won’t expect to find next to the paper towels. This insulated midweight jacket has the details kids actually use: an inner powder skirt, a storm shield inside the hood, and two zippered side pockets. The hood comes off when it’s not needed, and sizes run XS–XL for the growth spurts that make buying premium kids’ gear hurt.

Sources indicate that pair it with the snow pants for a budget head-to-toe outfit. The insulated pants are wind and water resistant, with snow gaiters and elastic grippers that keep boots from letting in snow, plus a Velcro-adjustable waist for the in-between sizes. Two front slant pockets, a side zip pocket and scuff guards at the hems round it out.

Compromise: With the jacket, you’re giving up the proven weather protection of a premium kids’ shell. The jacket lists no waterproof rating or sealed seams, so think dry-snow resort days, not PNW storm skiing. For the pants, water resistant isn’t waterproof, so don’t count on these for skiing and playing in wet snow.

Eddie Bauer has been making outdoor clothing and gear since 1920, when Eddie Bauer opened his Sports Shop in Seattle, close to Costco’s headquarters in Washington. The hooded full-zip fleece nods to the days when a heavyweight midlayer doubled as a jacket. Layered under a shell for ski days, or standalone, the 100 percent polyester fleece has a soft and comfy kid-friendly hand feel.

Compromise: This isn’t a lightweight performance fleece for easy layering under a ski jacket; its heavyweight fuzzy fabric makes it better suited to après play and around-town wear.

Industry observers note that at $50, the 32 Degrees Rechargeable Heated Vest is your gateway into heated ski gear. It’s the perfect marriage of value and warmth, and fits well over base and midlayers. Fleece-lined and lightweight, the vest comes pre-wired with four heat panels, two in front and two in back. A palm-sized battery pack, rechargeable through a USB-C charging cable, powers the heat, offering a little extra warmth for chilly chairlift rides.

Compromise: If you pay under $50, don’t expect the design and functionality of a $150 vest. Expect relatively short battery life, and make sure to research how to turn it on. Plus, all your friends will know when you have your vest turned on thanks to a red “Heat” logo. But embrace this: You will be warmer than them.

According to recent reports, 32 Degrees’ mission is to provide value and comfort, which is exactly why Costco skiers should take a hard look at the 32 Degrees Women’s Fleece. The high-pile fleece is not only soft and comfy, but it traps in body heat, while the 1/4-zip offers some venting. The kangaroo pocket doubles as a handwarmer, but what women may appreciate most is that the round-bottom hem looks cool with tights or snowpants.

Compromise: The sleeves are known to run long.

According to recent reports, spyder, founded in 1978 in Boulder, Colorado, is one of the most recognizable ski brands around the world. The Spyder Full Zip Sweater Jacket remains the quintessential ski town staple around every ski resort. Wear it as a standalone piece, or use the durable, heavyweight jacket as a midlayer under a ski jacket. Burly zippers abound with the full front zippered closure, a chest pocket and side storage pocket.

According to recent reports, compromise: The heavyweight fabric on this sweater jacket makes it a bit hefty for aerobic activities. Since it leans more après than technical, don’t expect great wind protection or core warmth.

Sources indicate that create a cool vibe during your après-ski tailgate with the Soundcore Boom 3i Outdoor Bluetooth speaker. Even if snowflakes fall, the waterproof and dustproof speaker keeps the beat without worrying about the elements. The rechargeable battery comes with a USB-C cable and holds a charge for up to 16 hours. At the end of a great ski day, the beat-synced lightshow hypes you up for more.

It has been revealed that compromise: There isn’t one. You get a tough, waterproof speaker at a reasonable price. It’s not a premium speaker for audiophiles, but it will get the job done.

According to recent reports, one of the best feelings in life is taking off your ski boots and sliding your feet into something comfortable. Enter the Kirkland Signature Unisex Slipper. Kirkland, Costco’s signature brand, named for the Seattle suburb where Costco began, is not to be scoffed at because it often stands in for other more expensive brand-name items like Uggs. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Southeastern Ohio is known for its heavily wooded rolling hills and the significant bucks that live there. Margaret Fuller of New Plymouth has hunted a small piece of private land there for years, and it’s where she was hunting this past weekend. In particular, she was looking for a giant 200-class buck she’d come to think of as “the Monarch.”.

The significant deer started showing up on trail camera about a month ago, although only at night. He was hitting scrapes near one of Fuller’s favorite ladder stands, and that’s where she hunted on Friday.

According to recent reports, “It was bitter cold that day, but I hunted from the morning until noon,” Fuller tells Outdoor Life. “I went inside to get warm for a while, then went back out that afternoon and hunted until dark.”.

That day she spotted a smaller buck about 50 yards from her stand. The deer was working along a trail toward her, but seemed to sense something was wrong and slipped away.

Industry observers note that fuller returned to that same stand the next day — her birthday — anyway. It’s the same spot she killed a 178-inch buck in 2022 during the firearms season.

“I didn’t get on stand until about noon,” indicates Fuller, a financial program manager for the Ohio Department of Natural Resources, “because I was so cold from the previous day’s hunt.”.

About 3 p.m. she heard an ATV roaring on the neighbor’s property and she thought her hunt that afternoon was over.

Recent findings suggest that “But a few minutes later I heard something in the woods, and then I caught a little movement,” states Fuller. “I stood up, grabbed my crossbow, and saw it was Monarch.”.

He was at 50 yards and coming to a scrape along the same trail the little buck had walked the day before.

“I was worried the Monarch would spook, too, like the smaller buck did. I knew I had to shoot soon before he caught my wind.”.

The buck began stopped to rub his rack on a tree, then started walking closer to Fuller.

Recent findings suggest that “I knew I had to stop him before he got to the place where he could smell me, so I grunted,” claims Fuller. “He stopped when I grunted, and I shot him at 30 yards.”.

In a recent development, instead of running, the buck dropped right there. Her shot had struck the spine, and the deer didn’t get up.

Fuller called her sons and husband, then climbed down from her ladder stand.

“I was on cloud nine,” she claims. “I’ve been hunting deer since I was 14 with my dad, and I’d have given anything for him to have been with me and see this buck … And it was on my birthday, too!”.

The family helped Fuller snap photos and field-dress the massive nontypical, which had 20 points. Then they butchered the deer at home.

The whitetail, which Fuller estimates is 5½ years old, was scored at 213 inches by Buckmasters measurer Toby Hughes.

“I’m over the moon,” says Fuller, who credits her success, in part, to “sticking with hunting even in the coldest weather.”.

It has been revealed that “But the best thing is the joy of having my sons and husband involved in hunting. Everyone helped me and that family camaraderie is really special.”.

And, wouldn’t you know, 13 miles into the woods, the whole thing went kablooey, spitting coolant everywhere. Best of all, it was nearing the end of the day, and the sun was sinking lower and lower.

In a recent development, what could’ve been a deadly ordeal, however, was quickly remedied thanks to my trusty Garmin inReach Mini 2. I simply text my wife, “Help,” and she sent a handful of neighbors, who also happen to be backcountry search and rescue, to come, well, rescue me.

Sources indicate that since then, I’ve never gone into the woods without it, and will tell people they absolutely need one if they’re going on any sort of backcountry (and sometimes front country) adventure. And right now, you can save a bunch of money not just on the inReach Mini 2 (which we reviewed here) , but also the brand-fresh inReach Mini 3, the inReach Messenger (reviewed here), and a host of other Garmin inReach products during Amazon’s pre-Black Friday sale.

Review: Oboz Katabatic Storm GTX Winter Hiking Boots
